Appendix A Steering Vectors: Detailed Construction

This appendix gives the complete construction of the steering-vector primitives used throughout the paper. The abbreviated version is in Section 3.1 of the main text.

Linear representation hypothesis and goal.

A broad empirical observation in the interpretability literature is that many high-level behaviors of LLMs, such as sentiment, truthfulness, refusal, and task identity, are encoded along approximately linear directions in the residual stream [1, 10, 2, 3]. This motivates the goal of finding, at each layer ℓ\ell, a single direction v(ℓ)∈ℝdv^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that shifting the hidden state along v(ℓ)v^{(\ell)} predictably shifts the corresponding behavior in the model’s output without any parameter update. Building v(ℓ)v^{(\ell)} requires two ingredients: a way to summarize the hidden state produced on a response as one vector per layer, and a pair of response populations whose summaries contrast in the target behavior.

Answer-token pooling.

A common choice for the per-response summary is the mean hidden state over the response tokens, masked to exclude the prompt. For a response of length TT with answer mask m∈{0,1}Tm\in\{0,1\}^{T}, the answer-token mean hidden state at layer ℓ\ell is

h¯(ℓ)​(x,y)=∑t=1Tmt​h(ℓ)​(x,y<t)∑t=1Tmt∈ℝd.\bar{h}^{(\ell)}(x,y)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}m_{t}\,h^{(\ell)}(x,y_{<t})}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}m_{t}}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d}. (13)

This collapses token-level variation into a single direction per layer and is the standard summary used in representation-level analyses of LLMs.

Difference-in-means steering vector.

Given two matched response populations 𝒟+\mathcal{D}_{+} and 𝒟−\mathcal{D}_{-} that differ in the target behavior, the standard recipe [1, 2, 3] sets v(ℓ)v^{(\ell)} to the difference of their answer-token-pooled means,

v(ℓ)=𝔼i∈𝒟+​[h¯(ℓ)​(xi,yi+)]−𝔼i∈𝒟−​[h¯(ℓ)​(xi,yi−)].v^{(\ell)}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{+}}\!\!\left[\bar{h}^{(\ell)}(x_{i},y_{i}^{+})\right]\;-\;\mathbb{E}_{i\in\mathcal{D}_{-}}\!\!\left[\bar{h}^{(\ell)}(x_{i},y_{i}^{-})\right]. (14)

We write v^(ℓ)=v(ℓ)/∥v(ℓ)∥2\hat{v}^{(\ell)}=v^{(\ell)}/\lVert v^{(\ell)}\rVert_{2} for the unit-normalized version. Under the linear representation assumption, hidden states in 𝒟+\mathcal{D}_{+} carry a larger component along the behavior-relevant direction than those in 𝒟−\mathcal{D}_{-}, while they share the same distribution along unrelated axes. Averaging over many samples in each population washes out the behavior-unrelated variation, so the difference of the two means concentrates on the direction that discriminates the two populations. Shifting the residual stream along v(ℓ)v^{(\ell)} at inference time then targets the same direction that was already correlated with the desired behavior in the training-set activations.

Additive injection.

The simplest way to apply v(ℓ)v^{(\ell)} to the hidden state at a chosen layer ℓ⋆\ell^{\star} is the additive primitive [1, 2],

h~t(ℓ⋆)=ht(ℓ⋆)+α​v(ℓ⋆),α∈ℝ.\tilde{h}^{(\ell^{\star})}_{t}\;=\;h^{(\ell^{\star})}_{t}\;+\;\alpha\,v^{(\ell^{\star})},\qquad\alpha\in\mathbb{R}. (15)

Additive injection changes both the direction and the magnitude of the hidden state, and has been reported to collapse the activation manifold at large α\alpha [22].

Spherical (Slerp) injection.

Spherical linear interpolation (Slerp) was introduced for quaternion animation by Shoemake [20] and later adopted for weight-space model merging [21] and for activation steering [22]. It avoids the magnitude-drift issue of additive injection by rotating the normalized hidden state ut=ht(ℓ⋆)/∥ht(ℓ⋆)∥2u_{t}=h^{(\ell^{\star})}_{t}/\lVert h^{(\ell^{\star})}_{t}\rVert_{2} toward a target direction ww along the shortest great-circle arc on the unit sphere,

Slerp⁡(u,w,α)=sin⁡((1−α)​ω)sin⁡ω​u+sin⁡(α​ω)sin⁡ω​w,ω=arccos⁡(u⊤​w).\mathrm{Slerp}(u,w;\alpha)\;=\;\frac{\sin\!\big((1-\alpha)\omega\big)}{\sin\omega}\,u\;+\;\frac{\sin(\alpha\omega)}{\sin\omega}\,w,\qquad\omega=\arccos(u^{\!\top}w). (16)

Taking w∝ht(ℓ⋆)+v(ℓ⋆)w\propto h^{(\ell^{\star})}_{t}+v^{(\ell^{\star})} gives the Slerp counterpart of Equation (15),

h~t(ℓ⋆)=∥ht(ℓ⋆)∥2⋅Slerp⁡(ut,w,α),\tilde{h}^{(\ell^{\star})}_{t}\;=\;\lVert h^{(\ell^{\star})}_{t}\rVert_{2}\cdot\mathrm{Slerp}\!\left(u_{t},\,w;\,\alpha\right), (17)

which preserves the norm of ht(ℓ⋆)h^{(\ell^{\star})}_{t} by construction.

Appendix B Hyperparameter Selection Protocol and Practical Guide

This section expands the selection protocol summarized in Section 4.2.1.

What was fixed, selected, and analyzed post hoc.
  • •

    Fixed in advance. The injection layer ℓ⋆=L/2+1\ell^{\star}=L/2+1 (mid-stack rule from inference-time steering [2]) for every model, in both regimes. No reported number comes from a per-model layer search.

  • •

    Selected on a development split. The injection operation (Per-sample Slerp vs. Mean-SV) and α\alpha were selected once on Qwen2.5-1.5B with GSM8K, training on 6,0006{,}000 training examples and validating on the remaining training examples. This gives Per-sample Slerp at α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and Mean-SV at α=0.5\alpha=0.5, which are then reused for every cell of Tables 1 and 3. For RL, λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 is used throughout.

Validation-based layer selection for a new backbone.

When adapting to a new architecture, we recommend a quarter-epoch (0.250.25) sweep over candidate layers, using the last 500500 training examples as the validation set and picking the best-validation layer. The total cost is roughly one extra epoch of training spread over the candidates. On Qwen2.5-1.5B this recovers ℓ⋆=15\ell^{\star}=15, which is also the test optimum, and on Llama-3.2-3B it recovers ℓ⋆=10\ell^{\star}=10, one of its two tied peaks, without access to test data. The same protocol applies to α\alpha.

Practical heuristics.
  • •

    Layer. Start mid-stack; across both families we tested, effective layers lie in the middle of the network and neither shallow nor deep layers are ever optimal. Use the quarter-epoch sweep above if budget allows.

  • •

    Operation and α\alpha. With no tuning budget, Mean-SV at α=0.5\alpha=0.5 is the safer choice because of its broad α\alpha plateau. Per-sample Slerp has a higher peak at α=0.1\alpha=0.1 but degrades quickly beyond α=0.3\alpha=0.3, falling below Plain at α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and collapsing at α=1\alpha=1 (Fig. 2(a)), so we advise keeping α≤0.3\alpha\leq 0.3 for Slerp.

  • •

    Large off-policy gaps. With thinking-mode teachers, ∥v∥\lVert v\rVert is roughly 3×3\times larger (Fig. 5), and the raw-norm default under-injects; a unit-normalized direction with α\alpha around 11–3×3\times the raw norm is a good starting point.

  • •

    When not to use the reference direction. If the per-sample directions are dispersed (low mean cos⁡(δi,v)\cos(\delta_{i},v), e.g. 0.480.48 on MBPP versus 0.810.81 on GSM8K), the reference direction likely encodes style rather than correctness; an outcome-conditioned direction (pass minus fail) is preferable.

Appendix C More Analysis on SFT Experiments

Here, we provide more ablation studies and further analysis.

MBPP redesign with execution-conditioned SV. The reference-based direction is a poor target on MBPP for two reasons. First, the per-sample δi\delta_{i} alignment is only 0.4830.483 on MBPP versus 0.8080.808 on GSM8K, so the direction is dispersed. Second, the cosine between the reference direction vrefv_{\mathrm{ref}} and the execution-conditioned direction vexec=𝔼⁡[h∣pass]−𝔼⁡[h∣fail]v_{\mathrm{exec}}=\mathbb{E}[h\mid\text{pass}]-\mathbb{E}[h\mid\text{fail}], which partitions the population by whether the bootstrap prediction passes the unit tests, is −0.447-0.447 at ℓ⋆=15\ell^{\star}=15 on Qwen2.5-1.5B and −0.437-0.437 on Qwen2.5-7B. In other words, reference-SV actively pushes the model away from the test-passing direction, and 100%100\% of passing bootstrap predictions differ syntactically from the reference solution, so the reference target carries arbitrary style on top of correctness. Switching to vexecv_{\mathrm{exec}} at α=0.3\alpha=0.3 on Qwen2.5-7B raises MBPP accuracy from 64.80%64.80\% (Plain SFT) to 66.00%66.00\%, a +1.20+1.20pp gain that is the first non-noise positive on MBPP in the entire study, with α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and α=0.5\alpha=0.5 giving smaller positives (65.20%65.20\% and 65.40%65.40\% respectively).

C.1 Training-Time vs. Inference-Time SV

Setup.

The inference-time SV is deliberately the same direction used in training, namely the Mean-SV reference-minus-prediction direction at layer ℓ⋆=L/2+1\ell^{\star}=L/2+1, added with coefficient α\alpha. We do not claim this is a good inference-time steering vector; the purpose of the experiment is to separate the two uses of one direction. Table 7 extends panel (c) of Fig. 2 to six cells.

Evidence for the offload account.

(i) Activation change. With the SV active during training, the change that training makes to the layer-15 hidden state on training answer tokens has cosine ≈−0.05\approx-0.05 with the SV direction, whereas SV-free training produces a clearly positive alignment. (ii) LoRA absorption check. A natural worry is that the adapter simply learns to undo the injection. Plain and SV-trained LoRA deltas have identical Frobenius norm to within 1%1\% across all three students (1.5B 19.3019.29=1.000\frac{19.30}{19.29}=1.000, 7B 27.8528.19=0.988\frac{27.85}{28.19}=0.988, Qwen3-4B 35.3835.55=0.995\frac{35.38}{35.55}=0.995), and the projection of the SV-trained LoRA delta onto vv is ≈10−6\approx 10^{-6}. The adapter therefore learns corrections overwhelmingly orthogonal to the SV, so the gain comes from redirected gradients rather than from magnitude inflation or from cancelling the injection. Together, these suggest that the SV supplies the component of the reference shift along its own direction (largely style and format) during training, so the parameters need not learn it; re-adding it at inference then only perturbs the hidden states.

A falsifiable prediction.

If the offload account is right, a configuration whose vector steers more strongly at inference supplies the target component more completely during the training forward pass, so offloading should also be more complete. Fixing the SV construction and varying the configuration (injection layer or strength), the inference-time steering effect of each configuration on the frozen model should therefore correlate positively with how much of the target behavior the corresponding trained model offloads, measured by the alignment of its learned update with the SV. We leave this causal test to future work.

Implication for placement.

The same account suggests why the best layer is model-specific. If the SV helps by offloading correctness-irrelevant information, the most effective injection layer is the one where the vector offloads the most such information. The best layer is then not purely a property of the architecture, since it also depends on how the training-time vector is constructed, since what can be offloaded is set by the vector itself.

C.2 Full Variant Sweep on SV-Augmented SFT

This appendix reports the full set of SV injection variants we tested on Qwen2.5-1.5B with GSM8K at ℓ⋆=15\ell^{\star}=15, in addition to the representative variants discussed in the main text. All variants below apply some form of steering vector throughout training; methods that disable the SV hook or use no SV at all are excluded by construction. The full numerical results are in Table 8; we group the variants by which of the three design axes from Section 4.1 they perturb, namely direction, placement, or operation.

Direction-axis variants.

The variants below modify how the injected direction vℓ⋆v^{\ell^{\star}} is constructed.

  • •

    Cos-weighted Mean-SV reweights each sample’s contribution to vmeanv_{\mathrm{mean}} by cos⁡(δi,vmean)\cos(\delta_{i},v_{\mathrm{mean}}), so that samples whose per-sample direction is well aligned with the global mean count more.

  • •

    Calc-wrong-only Mean-SV builds vmeanv_{\mathrm{mean}} from only the samples whose bootstrap prediction has a wrong final answer, on the hypothesis that wrong samples carry the most useful correction direction.

  • •

    Clean-SV (consolidated) keeps only the samples with cos⁡(δi,vmean)>0.3\cos(\delta_{i},v_{\mathrm{mean}})>0.3 and recomputes the mean from this clean subset, then injects the consolidated direction on every training sample.

  • •

    PCA PC1 SV (also reported in the main text) replaces vmeanv_{\mathrm{mean}} with the first principal component of the per-sample δi\delta_{i} matrix.

  • •

    Dynamic SV recomputes the steering vector online during training. Every 200200 optimizer steps we re-run the training set through the current LoRA-adapted model with and without GT teacher forcing, recompute both the GT-mean and the Pred-mean, and replace the injected direction with the freshly recomputed vmeanv_{\mathrm{mean}}.

Placement-axis variants.

The variants below modify where the SV is injected, namely which token positions or which layers.

  • •

    Slerp first-KK restricts the Slerp hook to only the first KK answer tokens, varying the front-loaded scope; we tested K=32K=32 and K=64K=64.

  • •

    Confidence-gated SV applies the SV only to answer-token positions where the next-token entropy under the current model exceeds a threshold, on the hypothesis that low-confidence tokens are where correction matters.

  • •

    Multi-layer (uniform) (also reported in the main text) injects Mean-SV at L∈{10,15,20}L\in\{10,15,20\} with uniform per-layer α=0.50/0.50/0.50\alpha=0.50/0.50/0.50.

  • •

    Multi-layer (tuned) injects at the same three layers with α=0.10/0.50/0.10\alpha=0.10/0.50/0.10, putting more weight on the middle layer.

  • •

    All-layer injection injects at every transformer block with the single-layer coefficient α=0.5\alpha=0.5. Training collapses, and the model emits an empty or truncated final answer on about 92%92\% of GSM8K test problems and scores near zero. We attribute this to the total intervention strength, since reusing a single-layer coefficient at every layer multiplies the effective perturbation, rather than to multi-layer injection itself. The three-layer schedules above train stably, but the directions at layers 1010, 1515, and 2020 have pairwise cosine ≈0.78\approx 0.78, so multi-layer injection largely amplifies one shared direction rather than adding independent corrections. Single-layer injection is therefore the simpler and more robust default.

Operation-axis variants.

The variants below modify how the SV combines with the existing hidden state, including the injection primitive, the sample-level gating, and the α\alpha schedule.

  • •

    Mean-SV additive is the standard mean-direction baseline that uses the global vmeanv_{\mathrm{mean}} with the additive primitive of Equation (2).

  • •

    Per-sample additive (also reported in the main text) keeps the per-sample δi\delta_{i} but injects it through the additive primitive rather than through Slerp.

  • •

    Negated Mean-SV additive flips the sign of the steering vector, subtracting α​vmean\alpha v_{\mathrm{mean}} instead of adding, to test whether the gain depends on the direction of the SV rather than on the presence of any in-place perturbation.

  • •

    Gated Slerp drops samples whose cos⁡(δi,vmean)\cos(\delta_{i},v_{\mathrm{mean}}) falls below a threshold and applies SV only on the remaining samples; we tested τ=0.5\tau=0.5 and the more aggressive τ=0.7\tau=0.7.

  • •

    α\alpha decay schedule starts at α=0.5\alpha=0.5 and linearly decays to α=0\alpha=0 over the epoch, asking whether SV is more useful in early training.

Discussion of the full sweep.

The full sweep reinforces the four conclusions drawn in the main text and adds three further ones. None of the direction-construction variants we tested exceeds plain Mean-SV by a meaningful margin, which we read as a consequence of the per-sample δi\delta_{i}’s being already 99.9%99.9\% aligned with the global mean on GSM8K (mean cos=0.808\cos=0.808); when the per-sample directions all point the same way, there is essentially nothing for a filter or a cleaner aggregation to recover. Sample-level and token-level gating (Gated Slerp at both thresholds, Confidence-gated SV) all under-perform the no-gating baseline, which we read as evidence that selectively skipping samples removes useful gradient signal more than it removes noise. Scope restrictions (Slerp first-KK at K=32K=32 or K=64K=64) hurt at every KK we tried, confirming that the SV signal is broadly distributed across the answer span rather than concentrated at the prefix. The tuned multi-layer schedule outperforms the uniform multi-layer schedule by a substantial margin but still falls short of single-layer Per-sample Slerp, which is consistent with the main-text reading that multi-layer injection demands careful per-layer α\alpha tuning rather than reusing a shared α\alpha across layers. Finally, the negated Mean-SV additive control matches the random-Gaussian control at roughly 55pp below Plain, ruling out the alternative that the SV gain comes from any in-place hidden-state perturbation rather than from the specific GT-vs-Pred direction.

Appendix D More Analysis on Distillation Experiments

This appendix collects the additional distillation analyses we deferred from the main text. All results are on the same 3×4×43\times 4\times 4 grid reported in Table 3.

Full off-policy mitigation sweep across all 10 cells.

The main text reports the four Qwen3-4B distillation cells of Figs. 3(a) and 3(b). Figure 4 extends the test to all 88 distillation cells of the headline grid (two students ×\times four teachers) plus the two SFT cells, in both the log-probability metric Δ​NLLsum\Delta\mathrm{NLL}_{\mathrm{sum}} and the linear-probability metric Δ​Psum\Delta P_{\mathrm{sum}}. The protocol matches the main text: we apply the trained-time SV hook (additive, α=0.5\alpha=0.5, ℓ⋆=L/2+1\ell^{\star}=L/2{+}1) to the base model under teacher forcing on 500500 sampled training prompts and report the per-prompt sums and the fraction of prompts on which Δ​NLLsum\Delta\mathrm{NLL}_{\mathrm{sum}} is positive. The two cells without off-policy mitigation (Qwen2.5-1.5B distilled from a non-thinking teacher) are exactly the cells where the headline accuracy table shows no SV-distill gain.

SV direction statistics by teacher.

Figure 5 reports three statistics for v(ℓ)v^{(\ell)} at ℓ⋆=15\ell^{\star}=15 averaged over the 1212 cells of each teacher, namely the norm ‖v‖\|v\|, the mean alignment cos⁡(δi,v)\cos(\delta_{i},v), and Cohen’s dd for the projGT−projPred\mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{GT}}-\mathrm{proj}_{\mathrm{Pred}} split. Both thinking teachers (Qwen3 thinking and Gemma thinking) produce roughly 3×3\times the norm, ∼\sim2×2\times the alignment, and ∼\sim2×2\times the Cohen’s dd of either non-thinking teacher, and the two non-thinking teachers are statistically indistinguishable on all three quantities despite being from different families. The two thinking teachers, by contrast, agree in magnitude on these statistics but produce different downstream gains, which is consistent with the cosine-similarity finding in the main text that their directions are not interchangeable.

Normalized SV vs. unnormalized SV.

Both Mean-SV and Per-sample Slerp inject the raw direction vv at a fixed coefficient α\alpha, so the actual injection magnitude is α⋅‖v‖\alpha\cdot\|v\| and confounds two factors, namely how strongly we steer and how large the underlying direction happens to be. Because thinking teachers produce SV directions with substantially larger ‖v‖\|v\| than non-thinking teachers (Fig. 5(a)), the same nominal α\alpha is not comparable across teachers. We therefore try Normalized SV, which replaces vv with the unit-normalized v^=v/‖v‖\hat{v}=v/\|v\|, so that α\alpha becomes the injection magnitude in unit-norm space. On the Qwen3-thinking ×\times MATH cell that produced the largest gain in Table 3, Normalized SV at a tuned α=15\alpha=15 reaches a +21.40+21.40pp gain over Plain on Qwen2.5-1.5B, up from +12.40+12.40pp under Per-sample Slerp at α=0.1\alpha=0.1. The full sweep across both Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B is shown in Fig. 6: the α\alpha-curve is monotonic and concave on both students, with the optimum in the range α∈[10,30]\alpha\in[10,30], which corresponds to roughly 11 to 33 times the raw norm ‖vraw‖\|v_{\mathrm{raw}}\|. Normalized SV at this tuned α\alpha beats Per-sample Slerp at α=0.1\alpha=0.1 on every think-teacher MATH cell we tested, so the headline number is bottlenecked by under-injection of the raw direction rather than by the direction itself.

Cluster separation as a predictor of SV gain.

The story from Section 4.2.3 that “higher Cohen’s dd implies more SV gain” breaks down on distillation. The three cells with the highest Cohen’s dd in the distillation grid are all Qwen3-thinking ×\times MBPP cells, with d∈{5.85,6.77,7.10}d\in\{5.85,6.77,7.10\}, but the SV gain on those same cells is in {−1.80,0.00,−0.60}\{-1.80,0.00,-0.60\}. Table 9 reports the top-six cells by Cohen’s dd alongside their SV gain. A high dd separates GT from Pred populations well, but only on the training distribution. For the gain to transfer to test time, the direction must encode signal that survives on-policy decoding, not just the GT-vs-Pred gap on training prompts. On thinking-teacher MBPP, the dominant component of the GT-Pred gap is verbose reasoning prefix versus terse code, which is a surface artifact rather than a transferable correctness signal.

Why Llama-3.2-3B underperforms under the canonical recipe.

The cross-family Llama-3.2-3B student gives essentially neutral mean Per-sample Slerp Δ\Delta across teachers in Table 3, in contrast to the consistently positive Qwen students. This is the same layer-choice issue that the SFT layer sweep in panel (b) of Fig. 2 already exposes, and not a failure specific to distillation. The Qwen-default rule sets ℓ⋆=L/2+1\ell^{\star}=L/2+1 on every Qwen student and lands on a representation regime where the GT-Pred direction is dense and well-aligned, but the same fractional depth on Llama-3.2-3B’s 2828 blocks (ℓ⋆=15\ell^{\star}=15) sits in a valley between two off-center optima. On Llama with GSM8K, Plain SFT is 62.09%62.09\%, the canonical ℓ⋆=15\ell^{\star}=15 drops the model by −0.30-0.30pp to 61.79%61.79\%, while ℓ⋆=10\ell^{\star}=10 and ℓ⋆=19\ell^{\star}=19 both lift Llama by +1.22+1.22pp to 63.31%63.31\%. A tuned distill layer of ℓ⋆=13\ell^{\star}=13 on the Gemma-thinking teacher reaches +9.0+9.0pp over the canonical ℓ⋆=15\ell^{\star}=15 on the same cell. The optimal SV injection layer therefore depends jointly on student family, dataset, and teacher mode, and is not a fixed fraction of network depth. Reusing a single-layer index across architectures is a confound that systematically suppresses Llama’s true potential rather than evidence that SV transfer fails.

Appendix E Analysis on Reinforcement Learning Experiments

This appendix collects the additional RL analyses that we deferred from the main text, namely two ablations that isolate the contribution of the SV direction and of the SV-Rescue advantage modification, and a layer-wise correlation study that supports the canonical injection layer.

Ablation 1: SV direction vs random direction.

We replace the precomputed correctness direction in SV-Rescue with a same-norm random Gaussian vector, holding every other hyperparameter fixed. Table 10 shows that the precomputed correctness direction beats the random control on both students. The SV-Rescue gain therefore depends on the direction being correctness-aligned and is not an artifact of shifting the advantage of wrong rollouts per se.

Ablation 2: SV-Explore without SV-Rescue.

SV-Explore stacks SV-Rescue on top of a per-prompt temperature schedule. To check that SV-Rescue is not redundant once exploration is added, we run SV-Explore on GSM8K with the SV-Rescue advantage disabled (temperature schedule only). Table 11 shows that removing SV-Rescue drops accuracy on both students, so the headline SV-Explore gain in Table 6 is the joint contribution of SV-Rescue and the exploration schedule rather than the schedule alone.

Combination with entropy-aware shaping.

Entropy-aware advantage shaping [9] also assigns learning signal to zero-variance groups. Over three seeds on Qwen2.5-1.5B with GSM8K, GRPO reaches 77.60±0.5177.60\pm 0.51, GRPO with SV-Rescue 78.13±0.9378.13\pm 0.93, GRPO with entropy-aware shaping 78.64±0.8078.64\pm 0.80, and GRPO with both 78.87±0.5978.87\pm 0.59. Entropy-aware shaping alone is stronger than SV-Rescue alone, while stacking SV-Rescue on top of it gives the best result. SV-Rescue is therefore best viewed as a composable auxiliary signal rather than a standalone solution to the zero-variance problem.

Layer-wise SV signal.

SV-Rescue uses ℓ⋆=L/2+1\ell^{\star}=L/2+1 as the layer at which the SV alignment score is read. To check whether this is the best layer for the RL setting, we compute the per-rollout Pearson correlation between the SV alignment score at every transformer block and the binary verifier reward on a 20002000-rollout GSM8K hold-out, both before and after RL (Fig. 7). The peak correlation lies slightly above ℓ⋆=L/2+1\ell^{\star}=L/2+1, near 2/32/3 depth, although the canonical L/2+1L/2+1 retains 8080-90%90\% of the peak. To test whether the higher hold-out correlation translates into stronger RL gain, we re-trained Qwen2.5-1.5B GSM8K SV-Rescue at the peak-correlation layer; the peak-layer run reaches 78.66%78.66\%, marginally above the canonical baseline of 78.35%78.35\%. Layer choice is therefore a small additional lever rather than a major one, and the canonical L/2+1L/2+1 default works well across students.

Appendix F Additional Baselines

All baselines below use the same model (Qwen2.5-1.5B), data, LoRA configuration, one-epoch budget, and evaluation protocol as our method.

Supervised baselines.

Table 12 compares the SV with two baselines that also target the off-policy mismatch of SFT. DFT [31] acts at the level of the objective, whereas the SV acts on the representation. With its original hyperparameters, DFT barely changes Plain under our LoRA setting; re-tuned for LoRA, it reaches 61.09%61.09\%, still below the SV. Adding the SV on top of DFT yields +3.76+3.76pp over DFT, so the representation-level correction is not subsumed by the objective-level one. A per-token hidden-state matching loss instead hurts accuracy, so explicitly pulling hidden states toward the reference does not replace injecting the direction.

DFT [31].

DFT rescales each token’s cross-entropy loss by the token’s detached probability under the current model, which corrects the off-policy mismatch at the level of the objective. We first used the hyperparameters recommended in the original paper, which were developed for full-parameter fine-tuning on different models and datasets and transfer poorly to our LoRA setting (58.88%58.88\%). We then re-searched DFT’s hyperparameters under our setting, reaching 61.09%61.09\%. DFT + SV uses DFT with its original hyperparameters, applying our Per-sample Slerp hook in the forward pass and the DFT loss in the objective.

Hidden-state distillation.

This baseline asks whether explicitly pulling hidden states toward the reference with an auxiliary loss can replace injecting the direction; it reduces accuracy to 53.68%53.68\%.

Entropy-aware advantage shaping [9].

This method assigns token-level advantages to zero-variance prompts based on token entropy, so all-wrong groups also contribute gradient. Entropy-aware + SV-Rescue adds the SV-Rescue term of Eq. 12 on top of the entropy-aware advantages.

Relation of the three-seed RL runs to Table 6.

The three-seed GRPO runs are an independent rerun with the same configuration; their means (77.6077.60 for GRPO and 78.1378.13 for SV-Rescue) differ slightly from the single-seed values in Table 6 (77.7277.72 and 78.3578.35).

Appendix G Discussion

Our results reveal a consistent set of conditions under which steering vectors provide a useful training signal, as well as clear boundaries where they do not.

When does SV injection help?

The largest and most reliable gains appear on reasoning tasks (GSM8K, MATH) where the off-policy gap between the model’s native style and the reference completion is large and directionally coherent. Per-sample Slerp exploits per-instance heterogeneity in this gap and outperforms the global Mean-SV direction on most cells, while Mean-SV remains competitive on the rest. In distillation, thinking-mode teachers amplify the benefit because their long reasoning traces widen the stylistic contrast and give the SV a richer correction signal. In RL, SV-Rescue recovers gradient on all-wrong groups that would otherwise contribute nothing to learning, and composes cleanly with orthogonal rollout-side mechanisms and with entropy-aware advantage shaping. Its standalone gain is small and below entropy-aware shaping alone, so we view it as an auxiliary signal rather than a standalone remedy.

When does SV injection fail?

The two failure modes we observe line up with two of the design axes from Section 4.1. First, code generation breaks the direction, where the reference-based SV direction is anti-correlated with the execution-conditioned correctness direction, so the SV actively pushes the model away from test-passing behavior. Second, cross-family layer transfer breaks the placement, where the canonical ℓ⋆=L/2+1\ell^{\star}=L/2+1 that works for Qwen lands in a valley for Llama-3.2-3B and requires a per-architecture layer search.

Training-time SV is internalized rather than memorized.

A separate observation that does not fit cleanly into the three-axis decomposition is that a model trained with Per-sample Slerp performs best at inference without SV, even though it was trained with SV active at every answer-token position. This indicates that the SV does not act as a permanent crutch the model leans on at decode time. Instead, the SV redirects the gradient during training so that the corrected behavior is internalized into the parameters themselves, and the resulting checkpoint generalizes beyond the steered training distribution rather than being tied to it. Section 4.2.3 and Section C.1 analyze this shift and show that the learned update is nearly orthogonal to the SV, which is consistent with the SV offloading a correctness-irrelevant component during training. A causal test of this offload account is the main open question we leave to future work.

Future directions: finer-grained steering vectors.

The directions we use in this work are coarse correctness summaries, namely the GT-vs-Pred displacement in SFT and the correct-vs-wrong contrast in RL. A natural next step is to partition the contrast populations more finely, for example, by execution outcome on code, by reasoning style, by task subtype, or by specific failure mode. Each finer direction could be activated selectively to shape what the model learns at a per-skill or per-mistake level rather than uniformly correcting toward a single reference style. The same machinery could also control the learning dynamics themselves, varying which directions fire and at what strength as training progresses, rather than fixing a single α\alpha and direction throughout. We see steering vectors as a general controller of post-training learning dynamics, of which the two regimes in this paper are only the first instances.

Limitations.

Our study has several limitations. First, all experiments use student models at or below 7B parameters; whether the findings transfer to larger scales remains open. Second, the best injection layer is model-specific; the fixed mid-stack rule is a reasonable default and the quarter-epoch validation sweep of Appendix B finds a better layer cheaply, but there is no principled criterion that predicts it without training. Third, our baseline comparison does not cover on-policy distillation, scheduled sampling, or gold-rollout repair, and in RL, SV-Rescue alone is weaker than entropy-aware shaping alone.

Appendix H Broader Impact

Our work studies activation-steering as a training signal for LLM post-training. The positive impact is a potentially better way of post-training. The negative impact is the general dual-use concern that any improvement to LLM reasoning capability can, in principle, be applied to harmful tasks. Our methods do not introduce a new direct path to such misuse beyond what already exists for the public base models we fine-tune. The SV directions we use encode model-vs-reference correctness rather than safety-relevant attributes such as refusal or compliance, so the technique is not a method for bypassing safety alignment.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and Section 1 accurately reflect the contribution.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: We show the negative results in the experimental part and also discuss more limitations in the appendix discussion part.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [N/A]

  14. Justification: No theory

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: We provide the information in the experimental part.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: The code link is given in the footnote on the first page.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: In the experimental part

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: Section 4.4 and Section 5.2.3 report mean ±\pm standard deviation over three training seeds for representative supervised, distillation, code, and RL settings. The full result grids in Tables 1–6 are single-seed, which we state in the limitations.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: in the SFT experimental part. We use the same setting for every part.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: [N/A]

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: In the appendix

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.
